2023_044_8_a_troy_school_district_direct.paragraph: An Independent Contractor Agreement between Secure Education Consultants, LLC (SEC) of 4527 Cascade Rd., Suite B, Grand Rapids, MI 49546 and the Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098, under which SEC furnishes a Director of Security and related security services. The term runs four years, from July 1, 2023 through June 30, 2027, with compensation of $228,000 in Year 1, $235,000 in Year 2, $215,000 in Year 3 and $221,000 in Year 4. Either party may terminate at will on at least ninety (90) calendar days' written notice.
2023_044_8_a_troy_school_district_direct.page:
**Parties and structure**
Independent Contractor Agreement between Secure Education Consultants, LLC (SEC), a Michigan limited liability company at 4527 Cascade Rd., Suite B, Grand Rapids, MI 49546, and the Troy School District, a Michigan general powers school district at 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098. SEC serves as an independent contractor; no employer/employee relationship is created, and SEC consultants expressly renounce District benefits and are not eligible for District retirement programs or fringe benefits. SEC bears all salaries, benefits, payroll and other taxes, unemployment taxes, Social Security contributions and worker's compensation premiums for its personnel.

**Term, termination and payment**
Four (4) years, beginning July 1, 2023 and ending June 30, 2027; workdays are those worked by District Directors. Either party may terminate for any reason or no reason on at least ninety (90) calendar days' written notice, with the District liable only for services rendered through the early termination date. If terminated mid-month for services paid but not rendered, the Contractor must return the pro-rata portion of the monthly installment within three (3) business days.

**Compensation**

| Contract year | Amount |
|---|---|
| Year 1 | $228,000 |
| Year 2 | $235,000 |
| Year 3 | $215,000 |
| Year 4 | $221,000 |

SEC invoices monthly; the District may instead prepay annually or pay the contract in full. Undisputed payments are due within thirty (30) days of invoice delivery, in USD. Disputes require written notice before the invoice due date, followed by a meeting to resolve. Compensation excludes travel for on-site services under Appendix C - airfare, ground transportation, lodging and meals/per diem are reimbursable and invoiced as incurred. Other expenses require advance written approval from the Assistant Superintendent of Business Services.

**Services**
SEC provides a Director of Security (duties in Appendix B) plus Behavioral Threat Assessment services (Appendix C), staff training (Critical Incident Response Training, Tabletop Exercises, De-Escalation Training, Behavioral Threat Assessment Training, Investigations in Schools: Best Practices for Administrators, Crisis Communication Training), site assessments on District request no more frequently than every 3 years, the eSEC online membership learning platform, and targeted social media monitoring. Any additional SEC services require separate contracting and advance written authorization.

**Compliance provisions**
Criminal background checks are required under Sections 1230 and 1230a of the Revised School Code, MCL 380.1230 and 380.1230a, at Contractor expense. SEC may not assign anyone convicted of a listed offense under Section 2 of the Sex Offenders Registration Act, MCL 28.722; offenses under MCL 380.1535a or 380.1539b; any felony (waivable only with prior written approval of the Board of Education and Superintendent for non-listed offenses); misdemeanors involving sexual or physical abuse under MCL 380.1230(10) and 1230(8); substantially similar federal or other-state offenses; or any other offense the District judges a risk. Nondiscrimination language is required by MCL 37.2209. Student records prepared by SEC are District property; confidential information marked or identified as such (orally disclosed items require written notice within 30 days) may not be used or disclosed. SEC retains its intellectual property and grants the District an irrevocable, non-exclusive, non-transferable, royalty-free internal-use license. SEC must carry commercial general liability insurance or self-insurance in limits acceptable to the District. Michigan law governs, with venue in Michigan courts.

**Appendix C scope**
M. H. Coggins, LLC and Dr. Coggins lead a phased four-year behavioral threat assessment build-out across five phases, with 24 hours per month of effort in Years One and Two and 12 hours per month in Years Three and Four.
2023_044_8_a_troy_school_district_direct.verbose:
**Agreement and parties.** Independent Contractor Agreement between Secure Education Consultants, LLC (SEC), a Michigan limited liability company whose address is 4527 Cascade Rd., Suite B, Grand Rapids, MI 49546, identified as Contractor, and the Troy School District, a Michigan general powers school district whose address is 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098, identified as District. The agreement runs for a term of four (4) years and obligates SEC to provide a Director of Security and all other contracted services identified in the agreement. It was presented to the Board of Education as agenda item 8.A at the May 16, 2023 meeting; the version is dated 3-24-23 v2.

**Engagement and relationship.** The District engages SEC as an independent contractor. Nothing creates an employer/employee relationship; SEC and its consultants specifically reject and renounce District employment benefits and acknowledge they are not entitled to other District benefits. SEC is self-directed, determines its own methods and manner of performing services within District policies and budgets, and may never represent itself or its consultants as District employees. SEC agrees to develop a service delivery plan with the District and provide ongoing support.

**Compensation of contractor personnel.** SEC is responsible for all salaries, benefits, payroll and other taxes, fees, charges and insurance required by federal, state or local law, including unemployment taxes, Social Security contributions and worker's compensation premiums, attributable to each SEC employee or agent. SEC is not entitled to participate in District retirement programs or fringe benefits unless otherwise agreed.

**Term and termination.** The contract runs four (4) years, beginning July 1, 2023 and ending June 30, 2027. All workdays are defined as those days worked by District Directors during the term. Either party may terminate for any reason or no reason at will on at least ninety (90) calendar days' written notice to the address first listed. On early termination the District is responsible only for the director's services rendered through the termination date. Upon termination all Contractor rights cease; the District is not liable for incidental or consequential damages, lost profits, or costs for services not actually performed. If the contract terminates mid-month with services paid for but not rendered, the Contractor must pay the District the pro-rata portion of the monthly installment within three (3) business days.

**Compensation to SEC.** Year 1: $228,000 (two-hundred twenty-eight thousand). Year 2: $235,000 (two-hundred thirty-five thousand). Year 3: $215,000 (two-hundred fifteen thousand). Year 4: $221,000 (two-hundred twenty-one thousand). SEC submits invoices monthly; in lieu of monthly invoicing the District may pay annually in advance or pay the contract in full. All undisputed payments are due within thirty (30) days of invoice delivery, made in USD by an agreed method. Disputed invoices require written notice before the due date stating the basis for the discrepancy, followed by a meeting; unresolved matters go to legal remedies. Total compensation excludes travel and related expenses for on-site services in Appendix C - the District agrees to reimburse airfare, ground transportation, lodging and meals/per diem, invoiced as incurred and pre-approvable on request. Other expenses are reimbursed only if approved in advance in writing by the Assistant Superintendent of Business Services.

**Services provided and other services.** SEC provides a Director of Security whose major duties are listed in Appendix B, plus Behavioral Threat Assessment services under Appendix C. Staff training at District request, with SEC recommending a cadence in line with best practice, includes Critical Incident Response Training, Tabletop Exercises, De-Escalation Training, Behavioral Threat Assessment Training, Investigations in Schools: Best Practices for Administrators, and Crisis Communication Training. Site assessments are provided on District request but not more frequently than every 3 years. eSEC, SEC's membership site, provides self-paced video Critical Incident Response lessons and school safety fundamentals on demand year-round. SEC also provides targeted social media monitoring. Additional SEC services must be individually contracted at negotiated rates and require advance written authorization.

**Facilities, background checks and records.** SEC may use District premises and facilities, and the District reserves sole discretion to revoke any SEC consultant's or employee's privilege to be on school premises. Criminal background checks are required under Sections 1230 and 1230a of the Revised School Code, MCL 380.1230 and 380.1230a, for all persons regularly and continuously assigned to school facilities, performed at Contractor expense following District Board Policy. SEC may not assign anyone convicted of: any listed offense under Section 2 of the Sex Offenders Registration Act, MCL 28.722; any offense under Sections 1535a or 1539 of the Revised School Code, MCL 380.1535a and 380.1539b; any felony, except that with prior written approval of the District's Board of Education and Superintendent a person convicted of a non-listed felony may perform services if the Board judges their presence poses no danger; any misdemeanor involving sexual or physical abuse as defined in Sections 1230(10) and 1230(8) of the Revised School Code, MCL 380.1230; substantially similar offenses under United States or other state law; or any other offense the District judges a potential risk. All records and documents SEC prepares about students are prepared per District practices and are District property.

**Confidentiality, intellectual property and risk terms.** SEC may not use or disclose District Confidential Information, including student identifiable information, during or after the term without written consent. Confidential Information covers tangible material marked confidential or proprietary, or orally disclosed material identified as confidential at disclosure or by written notice to SEC within 30 days; carve-outs cover public domain material, information already known to SEC, independently developed information, and material rightfully disclosed by an unencumbered third party. District records, forms and supplies remain District property, returnable on demand or termination, and SEC is given access to and rights to reproduce Student Data useful in evaluating services. SEC retains all patent, copyright and other intellectual property in its methodologies, models, tools and know-how (SEC's IP), and deliverables developed for the District are SEC's sole and exclusive property; the District receives an irrevocable, non-exclusive, non-transferable, royalty-free internal-use license with no right to sell, copy, reproduce, make derivative works from, or alter SEC's IP or Work Product. SEC guarantees nothing about preventing, stopping or limiting threats, injuries or dangers, and is responsible for intentional torts or damage caused by its employees. The indemnification clause acknowledges the District, as a Michigan general powers school district, may lack authority to indemnify contractors; to the extent permitted by law each party indemnifies the other, surviving termination. SEC must carry commercial general liability insurance or self-insurance in limits acceptable to the District, with written evidence on request.

**General clauses.** Amendments require a writing signed by each party. Neither party may assign obligations without prior written consent. The nondiscrimination clause, required by MCL 37.2209, covers race, color, religion, national origin, age, sex, marital status, disability and other protected classes. Waiver of one breach is not waiver of later breaches, and invalid provisions are severed. Miscellaneous provisions cover complete agreement superseding prior negotiations; Michigan governing law and forum with consent to service of process by personal delivery; each party bearing its own counsel and accounting fees; binding effect on successors and assigns; no third party beneficiaries; no waiver by non-enforcement; SEC consultants' compliance with all District Board of Education policies, regulations and administrative guidelines; and mutual publicity restrictions requiring prior written approval before either party uses the other's name, trademarks or staff names. The signature block lists Secure Education Consultants, LLC as Contractor and a blank [District Name] as District, with unsigned name, title and date lines.

**Appendix A - Training.** Behavioral Threat Assessment: covers adopting a comprehensive threat assessment process, the assessment tool, identifying appropriate response to students in crisis, identifying team members, documentation of support, and integration into school safety; 90 minutes. Crisis Communication Strategies: best practices and tactics for accurate, timely stakeholder information and protecting reputational assets; 90 minutes. De-Escalation Training Strategies: recognizing verbal and nonverbal warning signs of increasing aggression, building rapport, managing emotional reactivity, communicating effectively; 60 to 90 minutes. Emergency Operation Plans - Tabletop Exercise: discussion-based simulation led by a senior consultant at the District's location, using guidelines drawn from the district's emergency plan, including coordination with local first responders and an after-action report; two (2) hours. Investigations in Schools: Best Practices for Administrators: questioning techniques, preservation of evidence, involvement of law enforcement and basic student rights, with scenarios; three (3) hours.

**Appendix B - Job responsibilities.** The Director of Security's duties include developing and implementing security plans for district events; managing ICHAT and employee fingerprint background checks; coordinating with the district communication team and media on school safety; providing monthly reports to the Central Office Leadership Team; advocating for the District on school safety grants and state aid; attending PTA, school board and community meetings; representing Troy School District in state and national security organizations; building safety and security training into new staff orientation before the school year; assisting with investigations alongside school and district administration; hiring and supervising district security staff in coordination with building administrators; developing and facilitating safety and training policies and leading staff training on behavior threat assessment, de-escalation and critical incident response; developing and maintaining EOPs, crisis response plans, BOE policy/guidelines and visitor entry procedures; training district and building-level administrators; creating building- or grade-level learning opportunities and video training; collaborating on site assessment recommendation implementation; serving as liaison to local law enforcement; leading the district's crisis and incident response teams; managing state mandates including emergency drill planning and reporting, emergency operations plan updates, suicide prevention and Ok2Say; coordinating annual AED, CPR and First Aid training; maintaining emergency kits including Stop the Bleed, Go Bags and student rosters; and developing security plans for events outside the school day.

**Appendix C - Behavioral Threat Assessment.** A phased four-year scope of work anticipating an eventual state mandate to establish behavioral threat assessment teams. Phase 1, Program Assessment: M. H. Coggins, LLC has developed a survey tool; tasks include customizing the survey for Troy School District (TSD) following preliminary discussions with the Superintendent and designated officials, with Dr. Coggins leading virtual meetings and structured interviews, then compiling and analyzing findings against best practices across eight program areas - threat assessment teams and specialized training, reporting methods for concerning behaviors and threats, triggers for the assessment process, investigation processes, threat classification methods, case management protocols, forms and documentation, and school culture and security awareness. Phase 2, Recommendations and Action Planning: prepare a prioritized report of recommendations and consult with TSD officials with follow-up briefings. Phase 3, Behavioral Threat Assessment Program Design: form a Risk Prevention Core Working Group of TSD administrators, school psychologists and social workers; execute an Action Plan with roughly one semester of planning and design followed by rollout the subsequent semester, with the first implementation year as a pilot; review Threat Assessment (TA) team composition; design a Multi-Tiered Case Classification System evaluating the CSTAG and NTAC frameworks and hybrids; evaluate and deliver specialized training; and advise on case documentation and record-keeping. Phase 4, Implement, Evaluate and Refine: roll out the program, use the initial semester as a pilot, measure effectiveness, and provide coaching and consultation. Phase 5, Ongoing Continuous Improvement: standardize threat reporting mechanisms, draft policies and operational procedures, plan community messaging and awareness, and provide ongoing Subject Matter Expertise consulting, recurrent staff training, case supervision and program oversight. Period of performance is a four-year scope, with Year One covering Phases 1 through 3, Year Two covering Phase 3 training plus Phase 4, and Years Three and Four covering Phase 5. Level of effort is 24 hours per month in Years One and Two, with additional hours subject to prior approval from the Superintendent, and 12 hours per month in Years Three and Four to support Phase 5. Retainer hours may be renegotiated if the level of effort substantively changes, and additional project-specific tasks may be priced at a firm fixed rate.

2023_045_6_8_math_adoption_may_16.paragraph: A May 2023 Board presentation recommending adoption of Illustrative Mathematics (IM) as the grades 6-8 mathematics curriculum for the Troy School District, condensing the longer May 2, 2023 Board workshop presentation. It recaps a 2019-2023 curriculum review, a two-semester pilot of Connected Mathematics Project and Illustrative Mathematics involving 50% of middle school math teachers across all four middle schools, and a redesigned middle school pathway in which the honors option moves to 8th grade as Honors Algebra 1. It also answers four community concerns, including that honors classes are not weighted in the Troy School District GPA.
2023_045_6_8_math_adoption_may_16.page:
**Context**
6-8 Math Curriculum Adoption, May 2023, following a lengthy Board Workshop presentation on Tuesday, May 2, 2023 that outlined the learning, collaboration in the field of mathematics, the curriculum pilot process, and supporting research. The full presentation is housed on the TSD Math website for community review. The curriculum review process spans 2019-2023 and included district data review of M-STEP program data over time, cohort data tracking student performance over time, and student choice and tracking data.

**Vision and findings**
The vision, citing NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics, states that all students are doers of mathematics and that the program should cultivate positive mathematical identities so students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy and beauty of mathematics. Finding 1: explore curricular changes - program data from the last 5 years preceding COVID showed student performance slightly decreasing or stagnant, with cohort data showing a decrease in students achieving advanced and proficient and an increase in students not proficient. Finding 2: explore course sequencing - students cannot fluidly move between tracks in middle school. Finding 3: explore classroom pedagogy - task-based, inquiry-based instruction building procedural fluency through conceptual understanding.

**Pilot**
The team investigated 8 different curricula and narrowed to two using a review matrix. 50% of middle school math teachers participated, with representation from Math 6, Math 6/7 Honors, Math 7, Math 7/8 Honors and Math 8, and all four middle schools participating. Semester 1 piloted Connected Mathematics Project (CMP); Semester 2 piloted Illustrative Mathematics (IM). Two or more units of each curriculum were taught by all pilot teachers.

**Recommendation**
Illustrative Math, described as problem-based, built on universal design for learning, with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners, extensions for students ready for more, built-in instructional routines, predictable and purposeful lesson structure, and practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review. Sample Math 8 lessons show a 10-minute warm-up activity with 5-7 minutes of independent work using the Collect and Display routine, a 20-minute activity with 15 minutes of pair work and a 5-minute discussion on negative exponents, and an extension. Every Cool Down is coded for teachers as More Chances, Points Emphasize, and Press Pause.

**Pathways and community concerns**

| Concern | District response |
|---|---|
| Structural change devalues math and removes recognition | TSD has a deep history of and commitment to excellence; the honors pathway moves to 8th grade with Honors Algebra I |
| Change may not motivate students to excel | IM gives teachers resources to meet student needs; teachers collaborate beginning in spring |
| Students may not be prepared for advanced and AP mathematics | Preparation should be as strong or stronger with IM |
| Course title change will impact GPA | Honors classes are not weighted in the Troy School District GPA, and middle school courses are not included in transcripts for college admissions |

**Standards crosswalk and implementation**
All Math 8 standards are embedded into Algebra I standards except the Geometry Strand. Honors Algebra I is anticipated to need approximately 4-5 weeks of instructional time to embed Math 8 standards. The school year has approximately 180 school days; the IM Algebra 1 curriculum proposes 140 lessons including assessments, leaving 40 days (or 8 weeks). Implementation includes two full-day meetings with Math 6, Math 7 and Math 8 teachers in Spring 2023, a Summer Institute August 8-11, and in 2023/24 back-to-school professional learning days, monthly job-embedded professional learning per grade-level team, monthly afterschool PLC meetings with after school pay, a full day of learning during January district professional learning, and a full-time Math Specialist in each building.

**Monitoring**
Goals: growth in students scoring advanced or proficient on M-STEP Math, PSAT and SAT; increased enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade; and stronger student problem solving and communication of mathematical thinking measured by internal common assessments.
2023_045_6_8_math_adoption_may_16.verbose:
**Presentation and framing.** 6-8 Math Curriculum Adoption, May 2023, presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on May 16, 2023. It follows the Board Workshop of Tuesday, May 2, 2023, at which staff gave a lengthy presentation outlining the learning, the collaboration within the field of mathematics, the curriculum pilot process, and the research guiding the recommendation. Community members are invited to review the full presentation housed on the TSD Math website. The 6-8 curriculum review process is dated 2019-2023.

**District data review.** The review drew on program data over time from M-STEP, cohort data tracking student performance over time, and student choice and tracking data.

**Vision for mathematics.** Citing NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics, the stated vision is that all students are doers of mathematics and that the purpose of the mathematics program is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy and beauty of mathematics.

**Findings.** Finding 1, explore curricular changes: program data from the last 5 years preceding COVID revealed that student performance was slightly decreasing or stagnant, and cohort data showed a decrease in the number of students achieving at advanced and proficient levels alongside an increase in students who were not proficient. Finding 2, explore course sequencing: students are not able to fluidly move between tracks in middle school. Finding 3, explore classroom pedagogy: explore task-based, inquiry-based instruction that builds procedural fluency through conceptual understanding. A review rubric slide accompanies the findings.

**Pilot process.** The team investigated 8 different curricula and narrowed the field to two using the review matrix. 50% of the district's middle school math teachers participated in the pilot, with representation from each course - Math 6, Math 6/7 Honors, Math 7, Math 7/8 Honors and Math 8 - and all four middle schools participating. The pilot structure placed Connected Mathematics Project (CMP) in Semester 1 and Illustrative Mathematics (IM) in Semester 2. The scope of the pilot required two or more units of each curriculum, CMP and IM, to be taught by all teachers in the pilot.

**Recommendation: Illustrative Math.** IM is characterized as problem-based, grounded in universal design for learning, with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners, extensions for students who are ready for more, built-in instructional routines that support teachers and students, activity and lesson structure that is predictable and purposeful, and practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review.

**Digging into IM: example lessons.** A Math 8 example illustrates cool-down guidance, with points to emphasize noting that if students struggle with negative exponents in the cool-down, teachers should plan to revisit negative exponents as opportunities arise over the next several lessons - for example in Lesson 6, Activity 2, "What happens with zero and negative exponents," inviting multiple students to share their thinking on negative exponents focusing on question 5. Every Cool Down is coded for teachers as More Chances, Points Emphasize, and Press Pause. A second Math 8 example describes a warm-up 10-minute activity in which students work independently for 5-7 minutes while the teacher uses the Collect and Display routine to stabilize the varied language in use during mathematical work so students' own output becomes a reference in developing mathematical language; not all students will finish all parts, and a whole-group discussion asks what patterns students saw, how they would continue those patterns for the last problem, whether anyone thought of it a different way, and what 10 to the negative 7 means in their own words and how it differs from 10 to the 7. A third Math 8 example describes a 20-minute activity with students working in pairs for 15 minutes followed by a 5-minute whole-group discussion, discussion supports for all students, selecting students who had disagreements to share what they disagreed about and how they reached agreement, emphasizing that exponent rules work with negative exponents, making a clear connection between exponent rules and multiplying repeated factors, and contrasting the expanded versions of (10 to the negative 2) cubed and (10 squared) to the negative 3. A fourth example is an extension in which students explore patterns to discover a rule that can be defined using an exponent that is not base 10 and that requires writing a number in an equivalent form using exponents. The deck also includes a sample SAT problem and a sample AP exam question.

**Middle school pathways.** Slides address choosing Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1. Math 8 is described as a natural transition from a Math 7 experience, in which students explore ideas of linearity, functions and geometry and establish a solid foundation for future work in Algebra 1 and Geometry. Honors Algebra 1 embeds Math 8 standards into Algebra 1, with students moving to formalizing and generalizing their understandings with a focus on efficiency and mastery. In the spring of 7th grade, buildings will host information nights to discuss and illustrate the differences between Math 8 and Honors Algebra 1 to help families make informed decisions, and families will engage with math teachers to discuss individual student needs, considering problem solving skills, communication of mathematical thinking and ideas, math assessment feedback, and standardized test scores.

**Community concerns and responses.** First, that the proposed change in structure in mathematics seems to devalue mathematics and removes recognition from students - the response cites TSD's deep history of and commitment to excellence, notes that the recommended changes provide access to a rich curriculum and a solid foundation of mathematical skills, and states that the opportunity to begin an honors pathway in mathematics moves to 8th grade with the selection of Honors Algebra I. Second, that the change in classroom learning may not motivate students to excel - the response says the IM curriculum provides teachers with resources to meet student needs, that teachers will collaborate beginning this spring to build skills in engaging and developing students' passions in mathematics, and that teachers are passionate about challenging students in math. Third, that students may not be prepared to be successful in advanced and AP level mathematics - the response states preparation should be as strong or stronger with implementation of the new IM curriculum. Fourth, that the change in course title will impact student GPA - the response states that honors classes are not weighted in the Troy School District GPA and that middle school courses are not included in student transcripts for college admissions.

**Standards alignment crosswalk.** All Math 8 standards are embedded into Algebra I standards with the exception of the Geometry Strand. The district anticipates that Honors Algebra I will need approximately 4-5 weeks of instructional time to embed standards from Math 8 into Honors Algebra 1 in addition to providing the Algebra I curriculum. The school year has approximately 180 school days; as an example, the IM Algebra 1 curriculum has proposed 140 lessons including assessments, which leaves 40 days (or 8 weeks) of time to embed Math 8 standards as needed.

**Supporting all students.** Advancement and acceleration measures include deep levels of learning, investing in staff through professional learning, enrichment materials embedded within Illustrative Math under the "Are You Ready for More?" feature, enrichment and enhancement opportunities such as math club and robotics, and traditional test-out opportunities to move more quickly through grade levels.

**Implementation plan.** Spring 2023 includes two full day meetings with Math 6, Math 7 and Math 8 teachers, followed by a Summer Institute on August 8-11. The 2023/24 school year includes back-to-school professional learning days, a monthly job-embedded professional learning experience per grade level team, monthly afterschool PLC meetings with after school pay, a full day of learning during January district professional learning, and a full time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach teachers, and provide intervention with struggling students.

**Support for families, 2023/24.** Parent learning sessions at buildings with math teachers, math specialists and CIS; parent learning sessions from experts in the field; and classroom video examples shared on the district website. Every IM unit includes a Family Support Materials section describing the big ideas in plain language, providing an overview of the mathematics, detailing what to expect as learning deepens, and including questions that promote conversation about the mathematics. Every IM lesson includes a lesson summary written to summarize the main mathematical points of a lesson including new vocabulary in student-friendly language, meant for students to read on their own time or to catch up after an absence, and useful for families seeking more detail.

**Monitoring success.** Three goals: see growth in the number of students who score advanced or proficient on the M-STEP Math Assessment, PSAT and SAT exams; increase enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade as measured through enrollment data and end-of-course summative exams; and build student problem solving skills and communication of mathematical thinking as monitored through internal common assessment. Measurement of student achievement may include annually reported M-STEP, PSAT and SAT results including cohort data, math benchmark assessments, unit assessments and common assessments studied with staff, student enrollment in Algebra 1, and student success as measured by grades in higher levels of mathematics.

2023_046_6_8_math_adoption_may_2.paragraph: The full May 2, 2023 Board workshop presentation on the Troy School District's 6-8 mathematics curriculum adoption, documenting a three-phase review conducted from 2019 to 2023 and recommending Illustrative Mathematics (IM). It records that the district has used Math Expressions and Big Ideas Math for almost 10 years, describes a two-semester pilot of Connected Mathematics Project and Illustrative Mathematics, and reports pilot teacher feedback favoring IM on manageability and support. It also sets out the tracking research base and a professional development calendar of full-day teacher meetings from May 30 through June 12 plus a Summer Institute tentatively August 8-11.
2023_046_6_8_math_adoption_may_2.page:
**Scope**
6-8 Math Curriculum Adoption, May 2023, covering the curriculum review process for 2019-2023 in three phases: Research and Vision, Explore, and Implementation.

**Phase 1: Research and Vision**
The district has used its current resources, Math Expressions and Big Ideas Math, for almost 10 years. Learning partnerships include Michael D. Steele, PhD, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee professor and National Science Foundation Program Officer; Ted Coe, PhD, VP of Academic Advocacy - Mathematics at NWEA and Director of Mathematics at ACHIEVE, INC. from 2014-2020; and Jonathan Bostic, PhD, Bowling Green State University professor of mathematics education. Data slides show 6th, 7th and 8th grade M-STEP results over time, noting that in the 2018/19 school year students took the PSAT 8, plus a cohort chart tracking the same students on Math M-STEP from grade 3 (2015) through grade 7 (2019), and a slide on students' opportunities for choice. Reflection covers the 8 Standards for Mathematical Practice and the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices, citing NCTM (2014), Principles to Actions. The vision cites NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics. Findings 1-3 identify curricular change, course sequencing, and classroom pedagogy as areas to explore.

**Phase 2: Explore**
A Middle School Math Curriculum Review Matrix organized in Blue, Red, Gold and Green strands asked about deep learning, student discussion, inquiry and task basis, storyline sequencing, standards for mathematical practice, valuing students' ideas, choice and voice, joy, differentiation, the 8 effective math practices, professional learning, research base, and future pathways. The team investigated 8 different curricula and narrowed to two; 50% of middle school math teachers piloted, with representation from Math 6, Math 6/7 Honors, Math 7, Math 7/8 Honors and Math 8 and all four middle schools. Semester 1 was Connected Mathematics Project (CMP), Semester 2 was Illustrative Mathematics (IM), with two or more units of each taught by all pilot teachers.

**Pilot professional learning and feedback**
Piloting teachers received 1.5 days of professional learning during the school day before each pilot, 4 job-embedded professional learning opportunities, and 2 days of district PD on best practice and pedagogy with Dr. Bostic and MSU facilitators; PLCs met with building subs, Math Specialists co-planned, co-taught and coached, and pilot teachers were paid to work after hours. Data collected included student and teacher surveys, work samples, videos and assessments. CMP celebrations cited multiple solution paths and collaboration, but teachers raised many concerns that materials were not manageable to use. IM celebrations cited invitation of all students, multiple solution paths, collaboration, manageable teacher materials, sufficient support, and teacher confidence to implement.

**Recommendation and research**
IM is authored and maintained exclusively by Illustrative Mathematics, a non-profit led by mathematician and standards author Dr. Bill McCallum, which began at the University of Arizona and was developed into a complete K-12 curriculum through grants from the National Science Foundation, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and the Carnegie Corporation of New York. The tracking research includes a University of Trento meta-analysis by Eder Terrin and Moris Triventi finding a null mean effect of tracking on efficiency but a positive effect on inequality, plus ACT research and an extensive reference list.

**Phase 3: Implementation**

| Date | Grade-level team |
|---|---|
| May 30 | Math 6 |
| May 31 | Math 7 |
| June 1 | Math 8 |
| June 5 | Math 6 |
| June 7 | Math 7 |
| June 12 | Math 8 |

Full day meetings with 8 subs each day; Summer Institute tentatively Aug 8-11. Middle school parent nights were held at Baker April 18, Boulan April 19, Larson April 20 and April 24, and Smith April 17, with a Community Round Table on April 13.
2023_046_6_8_math_adoption_may_2.verbose:
**Presentation.** 6-8 Math Curriculum Adoption, May 2023, delivered at the Troy School District Board workshop on May 2, 2023, documenting the 6-8 curriculum review process for 2019-2023 across three phases: Phase 1 Research and Vision, Phase 2 Explore, and Phase 3 Implementation.

**Phase 1: Research and Vision.** The district notes it has used its current resources, Math Expressions and Big Ideas Math, for almost 10 years, and that a great deal of learning has occurred in the last 10 years. Learning partnerships are listed as Michael D. Steele, PhD, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee professor and National Science Foundation Program Officer; Ted Coe, PhD, VP, Academic Advocacy - Mathematics at NWEA and, from 2014-2020, Director of Mathematics at ACHIEVE, INC.; and Jonathan Bostic, PhD, Bowling Green State University professor of mathematics education. Data slides present 6th grade M-STEP data over time, 7th grade M-STEP data over time, and 8th grade M-STEP data over time, with a note that in the 2018/19 school year students took the PSAT 8. A math cohort chart for grades 3-7 tracks student performance on Math M-STEP for the same cohort of students from grade 3 in 2015 through grade 7 in 2019. A further slide addresses students' opportunities for choice.

**Standards and pedagogy reflection.** The deck lists the eight Standards for Mathematical Practice: make sense of problems and persevere; reason abstractly and quantitatively; construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; model with mathematics; use appropriate tools strategically; attend to precision; look for and make use of structure; and look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning. It presents the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices as the means to implement the Michigan K-12 Math Standards, citing NCTM (2014), Principles to Actions: Ensuring mathematical success for all.

**Vision and findings.** The vision, citing NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics, states that all students are doers of mathematics and that the program's purpose is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy and beauty of mathematics. Finding 1, explore curricular changes: program data from the last 5 years preceding COVID showed student performance slightly decreasing or stagnant, with cohort data showing a decrease in students achieving advanced and proficient and an increase in students not proficient. Finding 2, explore course sequencing: students are not able to fluidly move between tracks in middle school. Finding 3, explore classroom pedagogy: explore task-based, inquiry-based instruction that builds procedural fluency through conceptual understanding.

**Phase 2: Explore.** Questions framed for the curricular pilot asked how TSD would align middle school math programming with its vision and beliefs; what world-class middle school mathematics programming looks like; how conceptual understanding is built and what learning trajectory students experience; what opportunities students experience in a task-based, inquiry-based classroom; and how a teacher can meet the needs of all learners in a collaborative, student-centered environment.

**Review matrix.** The Middle School Math Curriculum Review Matrix is organized into Blue, Red, Gold and Green sections, each with Evidence and Overall rating/impression fields. Blue covers Deep Learning opportunities, student discussion and talk, inquiry and/or task basis, cohesive topic sequencing in an engaging storyline or learning arc, and support for the standards for mathematical practice. Red covers valuing students' mathematical ideas, inviting all students in, choice and voice, eliciting joy, and differentiation opportunities. Gold covers support for teachers in using the 8 effective math practices, what professional learning is offered and how it is structured and who runs it, ongoing teacher support, support for differentiation, and connection to a research base or learning organization such as a university. Green covers support for students in future pathways and relevance to students' lives and college and career interests.

**Pilot process.** The team investigated 8 different curricula and narrowed to two using the review matrix. 50% of middle school math teachers participated, with representation from each course - Math 6, Math 6/7 Honors, Math 7, Math 7/8 Honors and Math 8 - and all four middle schools participating. Semester 1 piloted Connected Mathematics Project (CMP) and Semester 2 piloted Illustrative Mathematics (IM), with two or more units of each curriculum taught by all pilot teachers. Both curricula were described as task-based, inquiry instruction with enhanced opportunities to access the Math Practice Standards, specifically making sense of problems and persevering, constructing viable arguments and critiquing the reasoning of others, and modeling with mathematics.

**Professional learning during the pilot.** 1.5 day of professional learning was provided during the school day to all piloting teachers prior to the start of each pilot, and 4 job-embedded professional learning opportunities were offered to every pilot teacher during the piloting experience. All middle school math teachers engaged in job-embedded professional learning around technology and the pilot curriculum, and during district PD all teachers engaged in 2 days of learning on best practice and pedagogy with Dr. Bostic and MSU facilitators. Pilot teachers met as PLCs supported with building subs, Math Specialists co-planned, co-taught and coached throughout the pilot, and pilot teachers were paid to work after hours. Data collected included student and teacher surveys, work samples, videos and assessments.

**Pilot teacher input.** For CMP, celebrations were that the curriculum provides multiple ways for students to solve problems, allows students to deepen learning through talk and collaboration, and that some teachers believed the support provided was sufficient to implement with fidelity. Areas of need included some concerns about the curriculum being invitational and relevant to students, many concerns about providing enough guidance because materials were not manageable to use, and some concerns about supporting the needs of all learners. For Illustrative Math, celebrations were that the curriculum invites all students into the mathematics, provides multiple ways to solve problems, allows students to deepen learning through talk and collaboration, that teacher materials provide enough guidance and are manageable to use, that teacher support was sufficient to implement with fidelity, and that teachers felt confident to implement. Areas of need were more guidance about fostering an engaging learning environment and more professional learning on supporting the needs of all learners. The team then revisited the review matrix.

**Recommendation: Illustrative Mathematics (IM).** IM curriculum is authored and maintained exclusively by Illustrative Mathematics, a non-profit organization led by noted mathematician and standards author Dr. Bill McCallum. IM began at the University of Arizona, where Dr. McCallum served as a professor, and has been developed into a complete K-12 curriculum through grants from the National Science Foundation, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the Carnegie Corporation of New York and others. IM is described as a research organization that consistently monitors implementation and impact, with a link to illustrativemathematics.org/impact/. IM is characterized as problem-based, built on universal design for learning, with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners, extensions for students ready for more, built-in instructional routines, predictable and purposeful activity and lesson structure, and practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review. Slides cover preparing for problem-based teaching and learning, the problem-based lesson structure, a sample SAT problem, a sample AP exam question, and school districts in Michigan utilizing or exploring IM.

**Course sequencing and choice (Finding 2).** District data showed students tend to stay in the track they are placed in throughout middle school, and it is difficult, even for students doing well in math, to move to the Honors track; the current structure requires families to purchase summer learning opportunities in order for students to move between tracks. IM is presented as enabling deep levels of engagement and differentiation for all math learners.

**Research base.** A timely research summary quotes The Effect of School Tracking on Student Achievement and Inequality: A Meta-Analysis by Eder Terrin and Moris Triventi of the University of Trento, reporting that applying meta-analytical techniques to studies from the last two decades yields a mean effect size of tracking on efficiency that is null while positive for inequality, providing no support for an equality-efficiency trade-off (quoting Skopek et al., 2019, p. 224), and concluding that de-tracking reforms which postpone tracking, reduce the number of tracks, or smooth out distinctions across tracks have potential to reduce inequality of educational opportunity based on social background without harming overall student achievement. Research from ACT notes that high school teachers often prioritize covering a broad range of advanced topics while college-level teachers think high school students should receive in-depth coverage of foundational topics like number sense and basic algebra (Chait & Venezia, 2009), and that students with a solid understanding of middle school mathematics are better prepared for advanced high school courses, improving success rates in college-level courses (ACT 2009, 2012). Two Other Resources slides list references including Boaler (2000), Bressoud (2017), Clotfelter, Ladd and Vigdor (2012) of Duke University, the Common Core State Standards Initiative (2010), Daro and Asturias (2019), Gamoran and Hannigan (2000), the Kansas State Department of Education White Paper (2015), Loveless (2016), Ma and Wilkins (2007), Morton and Riegle-Crumb (2019), NCEE (2013), Patall, Cooper and Robinson (2008), Rosenstein (2014) of Rutgers, and US Department of Education reports from 2012 and 2018.

**Middle school pathways and FAQ.** Pathway slides reference Grade 8, Grade 9 and Grade 10 sequences. The FAQ asks whether Math 8 content is being skipped, answering that Math 8 content will be intentionally and thoughtfully embedded into the middle school Algebra 1 course, work to be completed in partnership with the Michigan Math and Science Leadership Network (MMSLN) and IM. It also asks what information families might use to choose Math 8 versus Algebra 1, answering that buildings will host family information nights to discuss and illustrate the differences.

**Supporting all students.** Advancement and acceleration measures include deep levels of learning, investing in staff through professional learning, enrichment materials embedded within Illustrative Math under "Are You Ready for More?", enrichment and enhancement opportunities such as math club and robotics, and traditional test-out opportunities to move more quickly through grade levels.

**Phase 3: Implementation.** Implementation principles are that teachers practice IM's problem-based instructional model with integrity and believe all students are capable of learning grade-level mathematics; that teachers engage in IM Professional Learning with implementation support through IM coaching, university partners and a Math Specialist at each building; that school leaders and administrators understand and support the systemic changes necessary to change teachers' practice; and that families and communities engage with and support their students' learning. The 2022/23 middle school math implementation PD days are full day meetings with 8 subs each day, scheduled May 30 for Math 6, May 31 for Math 7, June 1 for Math 8, June 5 for Math 6, June 7 for Math 7 and June 12 for Math 8, with a Summer Institute tentatively August 8-11. For 2023/24, back-to-school professional learning will focus on using the new resources, with job-embedded professional learning with IM coaches throughout the school year, a full time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach teachers and provide intervention with struggling students, and monthly afterschool PLC meetings with after school pay.

**Support for families.** For 2022/23 to date, middle school parent nights were held at Baker on April 18, Boulan on April 19, Larson on April 20 and April 24, and Smith on April 17, with a Community Round Table to answer family questions on April 13, plus a video explaining the review process, curriculum changes and a classroom sneak peek, an Academics website, and ongoing one-on-one conversations with families. For 2023/24, the district plans parent learning sessions at buildings with math teachers, math specialists and CIS, parent learning sessions from experts in the field, and classroom video examples on the website. Every IM unit includes Family Support Materials describing the big ideas in plain language, and every IM lesson includes a lesson summary in student-friendly language covering the main mathematical points and new vocabulary.

**Monitoring success.** The district will continuously gather teacher feedback about supports, next learning and the implementation process, and measure student achievement regularly - reported annually via M-STEP, PSAT and SAT including cohort data, plus benchmarks, and studied with staff via unit assessments, student enrollment in Algebra 1, and student success as measured by grades in higher levels of mathematics.
